edition.deck: The first day of Ukraine peace talks drew cautious praise from Washington, while a deadly explosion in Spain and fresh scrutiny of US military movements in Britain underscore a day of unsettled security news. Elsewhere, Denmark debates school rules and sees signs of cooling apartment prices in Copenhagen.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises significant developments from the day, including the resumed Ukraine talks, the deadly incident in Spain, and new UK and Danish reporting. Repeated morning coverage is included only where the gather supplies a material new development or a distinct angle.

content.headline: Ukraine, Russia and US call first day of Abu Dhabi talks ‘productive’
content.shortHeadline: US calls first day of Ukraine talks ‘productive’
content.standfirst: The first trilateral talks since February ended after four hours, with discussions due to resume on Wednesday. Washington says the sides have shown some flexibility, but their positions on territory and postwar security remain far apart.

image.caption: Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.

sources.originalTitle: First day of Ukraine peace talks 'very productive', US says

segments.body: The first day of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi has ended, with a second day scheduled for Wednesday. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who did not attend, called the discussions “very productive”; senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow made no public comment.

segments.title: Major gaps remain
segments.body: A breakthrough is not expected. Moscow wants Ukraine to give up the parts of Donetsk it still controls, while Kyiv wants to freeze the front line. The US has said the sides have shown some private flexibility, but a security framework is also unresolved. European leaders are pressing to be involved in decisions affecting the continent’s security.

perspectives.body: Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko told the BBC he fears President Trump wants a quick deal at Ukraine’s expense. He argued that pressure on Russia, rather than concessions, is needed to bring it to serious negotiations.

content.headline: Police officer and police dog killed in explosion in northern Spain
content.shortHeadline: Blast in Oviedo kills police officer and dog
content.standfirst: A bomb exploded as officers examined a suspicious backpack after responding to a report of a shooting in Oviedo. A second officer was seriously injured; the suspect remains at large.

sources.originalTitle: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in northern Spain

segments.body: A police officer and a three-year-old police dog, Deny, were killed when a suspicious backpack exploded in Oviedo, northern Spain, on Tuesday. A second officer was seriously injured and taken to hospital. Police are searching for the suspect, who fled after a woman was found with gunshot wounds.

segments.title: What happened
segments.body: Officers from the canine and explosives-disposal units were examining the backpack after reports of a dispute between neighbours. Police said it had a flashing light. The package exploded as it was being moved outside to protect residents. The woman who had been shot was also taken to hospital.

content.headline: Epstein survivor says modelling agency sent her to his home
content.shortHeadline: Epstein survivor says agency sent her to his home
content.standfirst: A woman says MC2 Model Management sent her to photoshoots at Jeffrey Epstein’s Florida home in 2009, when he was serving a sentence for sex offences. The agency’s former US president has not responded to the BBC’s allegations.

image.caption: Roza has shared her account of being sent to Jeffrey Epstein’s home for photoshoots.

sources.originalTitle: 'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home

segments.body: A woman identified as Roza by the BBC says MC2 Model Management sent her to two photoshoots at Jeffrey Epstein’s Florida home in 2009, when she was 18 and had recently arrived in the US from Uzbekistan. Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was permitted to work from home.

segments.title: Questions about the agency
segments.body: Roza says the shoots led to her being employed as Epstein’s assistant, a role other survivors have described as part of his abuse. The BBC says documents show Epstein gave MC2 $1m in 2005 and that 10 models from the agency met or communicated with him after his conviction. The agency’s former US president, Jeff Fuller, has previously said he did not know Roza was going to Epstein’s home; he did not respond to the BBC’s latest allegations.

content.headline: Israel’s new parliament convenes as Gadi Eisenkot tries to form government
content.shortHeadline: Eisenkot begins effort to form Israel’s next government
content.standfirst: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible two-week extension, to build a coalition after receiving more recommendations than caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Neither bloc has a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

image.caption: Gadi Eisenkot faces coalition talks after being tasked with trying to form Israel’s next government.

sources.originalTitle: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government

segments.body: Israel’s new parliament has been sworn in, and President Isaac Herzog has tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with trying to form a government. Eisenkot’s four-party bloc won 48 seats in October’s election, against 53 for Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc; both are short of the 61 needed for a majority.

segments.title: Coalition arithmetic
segments.body: Eisenkot has called for a “national emergency government” and set out four principles for potential partners, including mandatory service and a commitment to dismantle Hamas’s military and governing capabilities. Those conditions could complicate talks with ultra-Orthodox and Arab-led parties. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister while the coalition process continues.

content.headline: Iran rejects France’s accusation over supermarket refrigeration hack
content.shortHeadline: Iran denies France’s claim over supermarket fridge hack
content.standfirst: Tehran calls the accusation “baseless and hostile” after France blamed Iran’s Revolutionary Guard for cyberattacks that spoiled chilled and frozen food. French authorities have not publicly explained how they attributed the attacks.

image.caption: Shelves were left bare after cyberattacks disrupted supermarket refrigeration.

sources.originalTitle: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking

segments.body: Iran has denied responsibility for cyberattacks that raised temperatures in French supermarket refrigerators and freezers, spoiling food. France said on Monday that it blamed Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and had summoned Iran’s ambassador to lodge a protest. Tehran called the accusation “baseless and hostile”.

segments.title: Attribution remains disputed
segments.body: French prosecutors have opened an investigation into the head of a cyber unit associated with the Revolutionary Guard and two deputies. The BBC reports that the attacks affected more than 100 Coopérative U supermarkets and 180 Intermarché and Netto stores, among others. France has not said how it reached its conclusion, and it is not known whether similar attacks in other European countries are linked.

perspectives.body: Iran’s foreign ministry says the allegation is part of an “outdated policy” of making accusations against the country. The BBC notes that cyberattacks are difficult to attribute because attackers can conceal their location.

content.headline: Nvidia and Jensen Huang sued by shareholders over alleged spy links
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia and CEO sued over alleged spy links
content.standfirst: A proposed California class action alleges Nvidia and Jensen Huang misled shareholders about the national-security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at customer Megaspeed. The claims have not been tested in court.

image.caption: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is facing shareholder claims over alleged disclosure failures.

sources.originalTitle: Nvidia and Jensen Huang sued in US over affair with alleged Chinese spy
Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy

segments.body: Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, are defendants in a proposed class action lawsuit alleging they misled shareholders about the potential business and national-security risks surrounding Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. The two are not related. The lawsuit is based on allegations that US authorities believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

segments.title: Investigation ongoing
segments.body: Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe its secrets or US national security were compromised, and its board has launched an independent inquiry. The FBI has declined to comment on the reported investigation. China has rejected the spying allegations as groundless. Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unknown, and the lawsuit’s allegations have not been established in court.

perspectives.body: President Donald Trump said he believed Jensen Huang when the Nvidia chief told him he did not know Alice Huang was allegedly a spy. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe its secrets or US national security were compromised.

content.headline: John Kerry says other countries must follow China on green energy
content.shortHeadline: Kerry urges world to follow China’s green-energy lead
content.standfirst: The former US secretary of state says China has accelerated its shift to clean energy while much of the world is “stumbling along”. At the COP31 talks, analysts say Beijing’s willingness to take a global leadership role remains uncertain.

image.caption: Sheep graze beneath solar panels in Qinghai province, China.

sources.originalTitle: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry

segments.body: John Kerry has urged the US and other countries to follow China’s lead in expanding green energy, saying the rest of the world is “stumbling along”. China is the world’s largest emitter but also a leading supplier of clean-energy technology; the Guardian reports it accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply-chain production capacity.

segments.title: Leadership and trade
segments.body: China’s latest five-year plan pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”, but analysts quoted by the Guardian say it has often avoided setting ambitious agendas at international climate forums. Beijing wants COP31 to discuss the free flow of green technology, amid disputes over tariffs on Chinese products. Researchers will watch for signals on climate finance and whether China will seek to host COP33 in 2028.

perspectives.body: Sustainability governance professor Yixian Sun says there is a mismatch between expectations of China’s international climate role and Chinese policymakers’ views. In his assessment, wider acceptance and trust would be needed for Beijing to take on more leadership.

content.headline: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.3tn in planned share listing
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.3tn
content.standfirst: The Claude chatbot maker plans to offer shares for $70 to $78 each and says it could raise up to $64bn in its Nasdaq listing. The proposed valuation is below some backers’ earlier expectations, as investors question AI spending and returns.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut

segments.body: Anthropic plans to offer shares at between $70 and $78 each in a Nasdaq listing this month, potentially raising up to $64bn and valuing the company at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn. The valuation is below the $2tn some backers reportedly predicted over the summer.

segments.title: Growth alongside losses
segments.body: The five-year-old company reported revenue of $16.2bn for the six months to the end of June, up from $1.1bn in the same period a year earlier. Its pre-tax loss also rose, to $80.7bn from $12.9bn. The planned listing comes amid volatility in AI shares and wider questions about whether heavy investment in the technology will pay off.

content.headline: French police make arrests in Mohamed Al Fayed abuse investigation
content.shortHeadline: Arrests made in French investigation into Al Fayed
content.standfirst: Several people were taken into custody and later released after searches at the Ritz Paris and other properties in October. French investigators are examining allegations including human trafficking and rape; the investigation continues.

image.caption: The Ritz Paris was among the properties searched in the investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed.

sources.originalTitle: Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say

segments.body: French police have made arrests in the investigation into allegations of abuse by Mohamed Al Fayed, the former Harrods and Ritz owner. Several people were questioned and released after searches in October at the Ritz Paris and other properties, including the Villa Windsor in Paris and a former Al Fayed property in Saint-Tropez.

segments.title: Survivors call for wider searches
segments.body: The Paris prosecutor’s office says digital material seized in the searches is being analysed and the inquiry is ongoing. More than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers since allegations against Al Fayed emerged. A survivor group welcomed the cooperation between French and British authorities and called for all properties owned by the family to be investigated.

perspectives.body: The advocacy group No One Above said the searches and evidence seizure reflect a serious investigation into a possible network, and called on the UK’s National Crime Agency to take over the inquiry. The Met has not announced such a move.

content.headline: US moves aircraft from RAF Mildenhall amid reported Iran threat
content.shortHeadline: US relocates aircraft from RAF Mildenhall amid Iran threat
content.standfirst: At least 10 US refuelling aircraft left the Suffolk base, with other assets moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath, according to flight tracking and reporting. The exact nature of the reported threat has not been disclosed, and officials say aircraft move for operational reasons.

image.caption: Military personnel load a US Air Force aircraft at RAF Mildenhall.

sources.originalTitle: US evacuates aircraft from RAF Mildenhall over reported Iran threat
US military aircraft leave second UK base

segments.body: At least 10 US Air Force refuelling aircraft left RAF Mildenhall on Monday and moved to other bases in Europe, according to flight-tracking data. The Guardian reports that Osprey transport aircraft were also sent to nearby RAF Lakenheath. The Wall Street Journal linked the move to an Iran-related threat, but that claim has not been independently confirmed by the BBC.

segments.title: Officials offer few details
segments.body: The precise nature of the reported threat remains unclear. The UK government says there is no immediate or direct danger to the base or nearby area. The Ministry of Defence and US Air Force have not confirmed the reason for the aircraft movements, saying assets move according to operational requirements. The US has also moved aircraft from RAF Fairford after an earlier suspected Iran-linked security incident.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that US officials have taken a risk-averse approach to threats against aircraft on the ground, and that UK security officials believe Iran lacks the capability to launch an explosive attack on a UK base. The threat level and its basis have not been publicly explained.

content.headline: Hegseth calls impeachment effort over Iran war a political stunt
content.shortHeadline: Hegseth calls impeachment effort a ‘stunt’
content.standfirst: The US defence secretary rejected allegations that he waged war without congressional authorisation and abused his powers. A Republican lawmaker’s resolution accuses him of unlawful military action and other misconduct.

image.caption: Pete Hegseth faces an impeachment effort over the administration’s military actions.

sources.originalTitle: Hegseth calls Republican’s bid to impeach him a ‘stunt’ by critics of Trump
Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Pete Hegseth
Hegseth: Rigsretssag vil vise USA's fjender, at vi straffer vore egne

segments.body: Pete Hegseth has called a bid to impeach him a “stunt” and a “farce”, after Republican congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment. Massie accuses the US defence secretary of waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers.

segments.title: Dispute over military action
segments.body: Hegseth says the operations cited in the resolution—including attacks on Iran and Yemen—were lawful, ordered by President Donald Trump and reported to Congress. Massie’s resolution also raises the killing of civilians, attacks on suspected drug boats and the capture of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro. The House is expected to take up the measure; any impeachment would send the case to the Senate.

perspectives.body: Hegseth argues that impeaching him would put US troops at risk of being prosecuted for carrying out orders. He says the allegations against him are politically motivated and that the operations were lawful.

content.headline: Argentina and UK clash at tribunal over Falklands oil project
content.shortHeadline: Falklands oil project brings UK and Argentina clash to tribunal
content.standfirst: Argentina has asked an international maritime tribunal to halt drilling planned for next year, arguing that the project deepens the sovereignty dispute and risks environmental harm. The UK says the court is not the place to decide sovereignty.

image.caption: Argentina’s president Javier Milei has called the Falklands oil project unlawful.

sources.originalTitle: UK and Argentina clash over Falklands oil project as Hamburg tribunal starts

segments.body: Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg to order a halt to the Sea Lion oil project off the Falkland Islands. At the opening of a two-day hearing, Argentina argued that the UK’s approval of drilling—planned to start in March—violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to avoid unilateral action while the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

segments.title: Arguments over jurisdiction and risk
segments.body: Argentina says the project could make a peaceful resolution harder and poses a risk of an oil spill in waters where it is responsible for search and rescue. The UK’s attorney general, Ellie Reeves, said Argentina was trying to litigate sovereignty through the tribunal and argued that the body does not have jurisdiction over that question. The hearing is the first time substantive Falklands issues have been heard at an international tribunal.

perspectives.body: The UK says the tribunal is not the forum for deciding sovereignty. Argentina argues that the oil project exploits disputed natural resources and would further entrench British control. The tribunal’s decision is not yet known.

content.headline: Bank of England deputy warns young people bear brunt of weak hiring
content.shortHeadline: Young people bear brunt of UK’s weak hiring, BoE deputy warns
content.standfirst: Clare Lombardelli says employers are holding on to staff but freezing recruitment in a “low-gear economy”, leaving young people struggling to find work. The Bank says another interest-rate rise in December remains possible.

image.caption: Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli has warned that weak hiring is hurting young people.

sources.originalTitle: Young people in UK hit by ‘low-gear economy’, warns Bank of England deputy

segments.body: Young people are bearing the cost of a UK labour market where employers are hiring less but not making many redundancies, Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli has told the Guardian. She described the pattern as a “low-gear economy” and said people entering the workforce are particularly affected.

segments.title: Interest-rate decision still open
segments.body: UK unemployment has risen to 4.7%, while youth unemployment has climbed to its highest level outside the pandemic since 2015. Lombardelli said the Bank’s December interest-rate decision remains “live” and will depend on the conflict in Iran, energy prices and wider economic data. She cautioned that higher unemployment would not necessarily reduce inflation if employers continue to retain staff and hire only for hard-to-fill roles.

content.headline: People in England’s poorest areas face more than twice the risk of early death
content.shortHeadline: Early-death risk is more than twice as high in England’s poorest areas
content.standfirst: Health Foundation analysis found 815 premature deaths per 100,000 people in England’s most deprived areas, compared with 353 in the least deprived. Rates also vary by qualifications, employment and region.

image.caption: The study found the largest regional health inequalities in northern England and Yorkshire and The Humber.

sources.originalTitle: People in deprived areas of England more than twice as likely to die early, study shows

segments.body: Adults in England’s most deprived areas were 2.3 times as likely to die before 75 as those in the least deprived areas, according to analysis by the Health Foundation. The study found 815 premature deaths per 100,000 people in the most deprived areas, compared with 353 per 100,000 in the least deprived.

segments.title: Differences by work and region
segments.body: The analysis also found that men who are long-term unemployed or have never worked had a premature mortality rate 3.5 times that of men in higher managerial, administrative and professional jobs. The gap was greatest in the north-east, north-west and Yorkshire and The Humber, and lowest in London. The Health Foundation called for action on education, employment and local economic conditions.

perspectives.body: The Race Equality Foundation cautioned that lower premature mortality in some ethnic groups does not mean those groups have better health or that racism is unimportant. It said poverty, employment, housing and discrimination interact with migration and ethnicity.

content.headline: David Walliams denies allegations in Guardian and ITN investigation
content.shortHeadline: Walliams denies allegations of grooming and harassment
content.standfirst: A Guardian and ITN investigation alleges that the entertainer pursued teenage girls and harassed women at work. Walliams denies being a sexual predator and says he has not broken the law; the court that refused his injunction did not rule on the truth of the allegations.

image.caption: David Walliams has denied allegations published following a court ruling on an injunction.

sources.originalTitle: David Walliams' career and controversies including Britain's Got Talent and Little Britain
What are the key legal issues surrounding the David Walliams case?

segments.body: David Walliams has denied allegations that he groomed young fans and harassed women in the workplace, after the High Court refused his attempt to block publication by the Guardian and ITN. Their three-year investigation alleges he pursued teenage girls and young women for sexual purposes. Walliams says he is not a sexual predator and has not broken the law.

segments.title: The court’s decision
segments.body: The court did not decide whether the allegations were true. The Guardian’s account of the hearing says the judge weighed Walliams’ privacy and family-life rights against the media’s freedom of expression and the public interest in reporting serious allegations. The court refused an injunction, and Walliams did not appeal by the deadline.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that the judge accepted publication could have a serious impact on Walliams’ private and family life, but found that the sources’ right to share their accounts and the public’s right to receive information on a matter of public interest carried substantial weight.

content.headline: Danish MPs consider broader powers for teachers to restrain pupils
content.shortHeadline: Denmark weighs new rules on teachers physically restraining pupils
content.standfirst: A bill would allow teachers to use physical intervention as a last resort when a pupil seriously disrupts lessons, as well as when someone is in danger. Researchers and parent groups warn of harm to trust and learning; the Danish Teachers’ Association supports clearer rules.

sources.originalTitle: Må en lærer tage fat i en elev, der forstyrrer? Nu skal Folketinget diskutere nye regler
Magnus blev holdt nede af flere lærere: 'Jeg følte ikke, jeg kunne stole på dem bagefter'

segments.body: Denmark’s parliament has begun considering a bill that would let teachers physically intervene when a pupil seriously disrupts lessons, after repeated verbal efforts to stop them. Physical intervention would still be a last resort. Under the current rules described by DR, it is permitted when a pupil poses a danger to themselves or others.

segments.title: Support and concerns
segments.body: The government says clearer rules would help teachers respond when situations escalate. The Danish Teachers’ Association supports the proposal, saying teachers need clearer guidance. Researchers and other organisations warn that physical intervention may damage relationships and make pupils feel less safe. Magnus Ivarsen, who says teachers restrained him at his former school, told DR the experience left him afraid and less able to trust them.

perspectives.body: Magnus Ivarsen says he understands teachers may need to intervene when a pupil disrupts lessons or behaves dangerously, but believes the restraint he experienced was excessive. His mother says the incidents have continued to affect him.

content.headline: Parents of Danish child with rare genetic disorder find hope abroad
content.shortHeadline: Family seeks treatment abroad for child with rare genetic disorder
content.standfirst: Karl Axel was diagnosed with a condition known in only about 11 people worldwide, and his parents say a specialist centre in the Netherlands and intensive therapy in the US offered new hope. His future remains uncertain.

sources.originalTitle: De troede, at deres søn var blind – indtil de fik en besked fra lægen, der fik deres verden til at bryde sammen

segments.body: Karl Axel was diagnosed at nine months with CAMK2B-PRO139LEU, a rare genetic condition affecting brain and nervous-system development. His parents, Emma Dahl and Niels Horvath, say doctors could not predict how it would affect him; the specialist who diagnosed him told TV 2 there is no clear template for the course of the condition.

segments.title: Seeking specialist support
segments.body: The family travelled to a research centre in Rotterdam and later took Karl Axel to the US for intensive physiotherapy. His parents say he made progress during those visits, but that daily life remained difficult when they returned to Denmark. They have also received help from a children’s hospice and now use overnight nursing support. The reporting describes one family’s experience, not a proven treatment for the condition.

perspectives.body: The diagnosing specialist says a condition with so few known cases can be difficult to treat in a small country, and that families may seek care abroad where clinicians have more experience with ultra-rare disorders.

content.headline: Copenhagen apartment prices fall for a third month, but remain high
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen apartment prices fall for third straight month
content.standfirst: Prices of owner-occupied flats in Copenhagen fell 1.1% in October, according to Boligsiden, even as they remained 12.3% higher than a year earlier. More homes are for sale and buyers are negotiating larger discounts.

image.caption: More apartments have recently been listed for sale in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Priserne på lejligheder i København fortsætter med at falde

segments.body: Prices of owner-occupied apartments in Copenhagen fell 1.1% in October, the third consecutive monthly decline, according to Boligsiden. The average price was still 74,638 kroner per square metre—12.3% higher than a year earlier. Frederiksberg remained more expensive, while prices in Aarhus continued to rise.

segments.title: More choice for buyers
segments.body: The number of apartments listed for sale has risen and average discounts have grown, giving buyers more room to negotiate than a year ago. A private economist quoted by TV 2 expects Copenhagen prices to keep falling, citing financing costs, energy prices and planned increases in housing taxes, but says it is impossible to predict the market’s timing precisely.

content.headline: Danish electricity prices surge, making EV charging time matter
content.shortHeadline: Charging an electric car at peak time can cost more
content.standfirst: Danish wholesale electricity prices have swung sharply, and charging an electric car at the most expensive time can cost up to 300 kroner more than waiting a few hours, TV 2 reports. Network charges add to the evening peak.

image.caption: An electric-vehicle charging point in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Så dyrt er det at lade din elbil, hvis du gør det på det forkerte tidspunkt

segments.body: Electricity prices on the European Nord Pool exchange varied widely on Tuesday, according to TV 2. It reports that charging an electric car at the most expensive time could cost up to 300 kroner more than waiting a few hours. The final cost depends on where and how the car is charged.

segments.title: Evening charges
segments.body: Winter network tariffs make electricity more expensive to transport during the peak period from 17:00 to 21:00. TV 2 says the tariffs are intended to shift flexible demand, including EV charging, away from those hours. The article notes that household appliances also use the same electricity, but typically consume less power than a car charger.

content.headline: Danish demolition dispute grows as contractor disputes MP’s account
content.shortHeadline: Demolition firm disputes MP’s claims over Klampenborg house
content.standfirst: A demolition company says a Klampenborg villa was unsafe to preserve, citing rotten supports and serious damage. The dispute follows criticism by MP Signe Wenneberg, who says the house should have been renovated and questions whether its materials were reused.

sources.originalTitle: Nedrivningsfirma går i rette med Signe Wenneberg: - Det stod på søjler, der var pilrådne
Signe Wenneberg gendeler slettet opslag: - Har jeg gjort noget strafbart? Nej
Husejer føler sig udskammet af folketingsmedlem Signe Wenneberg

segments.body: A demolition company has disputed MP Signe Wenneberg’s description of a Klampenborg villa as being in good condition before it was torn down. A machine operator who worked on the demolition told TV 2 that the house was crooked, had rotten supports and extensive settlement damage. A condition report cited by the broadcaster lists six critical and six serious defects.

segments.title: Competing accounts
segments.body: Wenneberg has argued that the house should have been preserved and has questioned whether its materials were reused. The demolition company says it sorts materials for reuse and that the building was taken apart by hand. The homeowner has said the house was not suitable for renovation; Wenneberg has apologised for an earlier post but later renewed her criticism. The accounts remain disputed.

perspectives.body: The demolition company says its workers have faced abuse and hostile messages after Wenneberg’s posts. Wenneberg did not respond to TV 2’s request for an interview about the company’s claims.

content.headline: Denmark tests a more contemporary translation of the Lord’s Prayer
content.shortHeadline: Denmark unveils updated translation of the Lord’s Prayer
content.standfirst: The Bible Society’s trial version replaces older phrases with modern Danish, including “our daily bread” and a rendering of forgiveness as forgiving others’ debts against us. The full Bible translation is planned for 2036.

image.caption: The Bible Society presents its trial translation of the Lord’s Prayer in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Her er det nye Fadervor

segments.body: The Bible Society has presented a trial translation of the Lord’s Prayer in more contemporary Danish. Among the changes, “our daily bread” replaces an older form, and a line about forgiving debtors is rendered as “forgive us our debt, just as we forgive others’ debts against us”.

The society says the aim is to make the prayer understandable to future generations while preserving its meaning. The wording is part of a broader new translation of the Bible, first announced in 2023; the complete edition is scheduled for 2036, the 500th anniversary of the Danish Reformation.

content.headline: Wynonna Judd’s new album turns grief and family upheaval into raw country
content.shortHeadline: Wynonna Judd turns grief into raw country songs
content.standfirst: After a decade away from albums, the country singer says making The Hard Truth became part of her attempt to heal. Its stripped-back songs address loss, family history and the struggles that have shaped her life.

image.caption: Wynonna Judd.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I went into a deep, deep hole’: Wynonna Judd on overcoming family tragedy and putting a lifetime of love and pain into her new album

segments.body: Wynonna Judd describes making The Hard Truth, her first album in ten years, as a “labour of love” and an approach to healing. She has left behind polished Nashville production for a spare mix of country, blues and soul, co-writing nearly every track and addressing life’s difficulties directly.

segments.title: Songs that face the past
segments.body: The album includes a song addressed to her mother, Naomi Judd, who died by suicide in 2022, and one about her biological father, whom she found only after he had died. Wynonna also speaks about raising her young granddaughter while her adult daughter struggles with addiction; she says caring for the child gives her a reason to look forward to each day.

content.headline: Rita Wilson’s new album finds her speaking more freely about age and identity
content.shortHeadline: Rita Wilson finds her voice on Sound of a Woman
content.standfirst: The actor and songwriter says her latest record traces women’s lives, from love and loss to illness and ageing. She also discusses Hollywood’s ageism and the creative freedom she found in music.

image.caption: Rita Wilson.

sources.originalTitle: Rita Wilson: ‘My body turned on me – but it was also there to heal me’

segments.body: Rita Wilson says Sound of a Woman is a collection about women’s experiences across a lifetime, including ageing, body image, illness and loss. She began pursuing songwriting in her fifties, after feeling that acting roles had confined her to familiar parts such as the nurturing mother or friend.

segments.title: A different way to speak
segments.body: Wilson says writing songs gave her a way to express things she did not feel able to say in acting roles. One track reflects on her body after breast-cancer treatment; another, she explains, is about breaking up with an earlier version of herself. She calls the entertainment business ageist and says speaking openly about it would once have frightened her.

content.headline: Richard Thompson looks back at folk’s past without putting his own story away
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson revisits folk, loss and a long career
content.standfirst: The Fairport Convention co-founder discusses his new solo album and the formative years behind it, including a 1969 crash that killed drummer Martin Lamble and Thompson’s girlfriend Jeannie Franklyn.

image.caption: Richard Thompson.

sources.originalTitle: Fairport Convention’s Richard Thompson on the crash that killed his bandmate

segments.body: Richard Thompson, 77, has released Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, his 20th solo album. He traces a six-decade career that began with Fairport Convention, whose aim was to make folk music sound distinctly British rather than follow the prevailing American styles.

segments.title: A memory that remains
segments.body: Thompson also revisits the 1969 road accident that killed Fairport drummer Martin Lamble and Jeannie Franklyn. He says the young band did not know how to deal with the loss and threw themselves into recording. Decades later, he says, he and former bandmates still think about Lamble.

content.headline: Manic Street Preachers revisit The Holy Bible and Richey Edwards’s absence
content.shortHeadline: Manic Street Preachers face The Holy Bible’s lasting weight
content.standfirst: James Dean Bradfield discusses the band’s live release of its bleak 1994 album, whose lyrics were shaped by Richey Edwards before his disappearance. He reflects on the pressure of performing the songs decades later.

image.caption: James Dean Bradfield, Nicky Wire and Sean Moore of Manic Street Preachers.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: The Holy Bible Live records Manic Street Preachers performing their 1994 album in full at London’s Roundhouse in 2014. James Dean Bradfield says its words, written chiefly by Richey Edwards, could weigh heavily on stage. The band’s live performance moves between defiance, anguish and a strange sense of triumph.

segments.title: What the songs carry
segments.body: Edwards disappeared in 1995 and is presumed to have died by suicide; he was legally declared dead in 2008. Bradfield says the band were young and ill-equipped to respond to Edwards’s mental-health struggles, even as they tried to help. Performing the album years later brought memories back, he says, but also gave the group a sense that they had done it justice.

content.headline: Fontaines DC’s rise began with ambition and a drive to keep writing better songs
content.shortHeadline: How Fontaines DC grew from Dublin students to a major band
content.standfirst: Teachers, promoters and early supporters recall the group’s beginnings in Dublin, where literary interests, restless songwriting and a clear desire to grow set them apart from the local scene.

image.caption: Fontaines DC performing at Finsbury Park.

sources.originalTitle: The breathtaking rise of Fontaines DC, by the people who were there

segments.body: Fontaines DC formed while its members were students at BIMM Dublin, bonding over writers including Yeats and Joyce as well as post-punk. Their early supporters remember a band with unusual focus: they arrived with plans for success and kept replacing songs in their set with new ones.

segments.title: An outsider’s view of Dublin
segments.body: The band members came to Dublin from elsewhere in Ireland and Spain, and early songs drew on the streets and daily life around Dublin 8. Their former teacher Alan Cullivan says their ambitions were matched by a determination to improve. Early promoter Aiden O’Connor recalls that the band’s energy was evident even in a small pub gig.

content.headline: The Go-Betweens’ turbulent story still invites listeners back to their songs
content.shortHeadline: Why The Go-Betweens’ complicated story deserves a listen
content.standfirst: Reissues and a new live album renew interest in the Australian group, whose literary pop and tangled relationships never delivered mainstream success. Their collaborators’ contributions, the feature argues, also deserve recognition.

image.caption: Robert Forster and Grant McLennan of The Go-Betweens.

sources.originalTitle: The messy, bizarre inside story of The Go-Betweens

segments.body: The Go-Betweens’ music paired Robert Forster’s sardonic writing with Grant McLennan’s melodic pop. A new live release and reissues bring attention back to a band whose songs, full of literary references and uneasy undercurrents, struggled to find a broad audience.

segments.title: A wider band story
segments.body: The feature traces the personal and creative tensions around the group’s 1988 album 16 Lovers Lane and its subsequent break-up. It also argues that drummer Lindy Morrison and multi-instrumentalist Amanda Brown were central to the band’s history, and notes that both have spoken of feeling erased from its story.

content.headline: Skepta’s The Fork and Knife turns grime legacy into a portrait of immigrant life
content.shortHeadline: Skepta connects grime’s past to a new story of Britain
content.standfirst: On his first album in seven years, the grime pioneer moves between familiar rhythms and new collaborators. The review sees a reflection on legacy—and on the opportunities his family’s generations worked towards.

sources.originalTitle: The Fork and Knife

segments.body: Skepta’s first album in seven years opens cautiously, revisiting familiar grime and rap sounds before widening into a broader account of his career. The review hears him move between styles, from a track with Aya Nakamura to a nine-minute cypher that gives younger MCs room alongside him.

segments.title: A legacy in motion
segments.body: The review reads the album’s title through the story of Skepta’s grandfather, who wanted his children and grandchildren to enjoy the comforts of the customers he served. That aspiration, the writer argues, gives the record’s reflections on success and immigrant family life a wider cultural meaning.

content.headline: Kings of Leon leave arena rock behind for a warmer, looser sound
content.shortHeadline: Kings of Leon make a striking turn on O My Beloved
content.standfirst: The band’s 10th album trades much of its polished stadium scale for spacious country-rock. The review hears a renewed maturity, even as some traces of their earlier sound remain.

sources.originalTitle: O My Beloved

segments.body: O My Beloved marks a sharp change for Kings of Leon, whose latest songs are spacious and acoustic-led rather than built around the arena rock that defined much of their later work. The band made the album with help from former Stills member Liam O’Neill.

segments.title: A return to looseness
segments.body: The review hears echoes of the band’s earlier, more intimate work in the record’s country-rock textures, while noting moments when old habits surface. It calls the album a largely impressive reinvention and says the group sounds looser than it has in decades.

content.headline: Ron Howard’s Avedon documentary traces a photographer drawn to revealing faces
content.shortHeadline: Avedon documentary explores the photographer behind the portraits
content.standfirst: The Netflix film follows Richard Avedon’s career from fashion photography to politically engaged portraiture. His collaborators describe a method built on conversation, trust and a willingness to make room for surprise.

image.caption: A still from Avedon.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects

segments.body: Ron Howard’s documentary Avedon draws on the photographer’s archive and the testimony of people who worked with him to survey a six-decade career. Avedon became known for stark white backdrops and portraits of figures from Marilyn Monroe to civil-rights activists and working-class Americans.

segments.title: Making space for a subject
segments.body: The film’s interviewees describe Avedon using conversation and playfulness to help people relax in front of the camera. He treated models as collaborators rather than props, and his assistant recalls how a chance moment of laughter from the Dalai Lama led Avedon to take the portraits he wanted.

content.headline: AI storyboards may save time, but artists say collaboration is part of the work
content.shortHeadline: What Hollywood could lose if AI replaces storyboard artists
content.standfirst: As film-makers experiment with text-to-image tools, storyboard artists and a film scholar argue that drawing scenes is also a way to develop a film’s visual language—and to make room for ideas that emerge through collaboration.

image.caption: A storyboard for Gone With the Wind.

sources.originalTitle: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?

segments.body: Generative AI is already being used in film-making, including by directors exploring its potential for storyboards. These illustrated panels help plan scenes and communicate a director’s intentions to cast and crew. Storyboard artist Alex Clark says the work is not simply about producing attractive drawings: it involves working out how a scene should be told.

segments.title: A process, not just an output
segments.body: Clark describes storyboarding as a collaborative stage in which artists, directors and other crew can test and refine ideas. Film lecturer Ferdinando Cocco argues that the drawings can also show how a film’s creative vision changes. Both suggest that the process of making and discussing the images may be a benefit in itself, not merely a step to automate.

content.headline: Whispers in the Woods finds wonder in a family’s quiet encounters with wildlife
content.shortHeadline: Whispers in the Woods takes a tender path through nature
content.standfirst: Vincent Munier’s documentary follows his father and teenage son through a forest in eastern France. Rather than explaining wildlife in detail, it uses patient images and a wistful score to explore how attention to nature can be passed on.

image.caption: A scene from Whispers in the Woods.

sources.originalTitle: Whispers in the Woods review – paddling in the moonlight in tender study of human-animal interaction

segments.body: Vincent Munier’s film centres on his father, naturalist Michel, and his teenage son Simon as they explore the Vosges forest. The film presents much of the journey through Simon’s perspective, as his grandfather helps him recognise the birds and animals around them.

segments.title: A different kind of nature film
segments.body: The review contrasts Munier’s emotionally focused approach with wildlife documentaries driven by facts and slow-motion spectacle. Lynx, foxes and deer appear in carefully composed shots, sometimes as indistinct shapes among the trees. Warren Ellis’s music deepens the film’s mood of quiet wonder.

content.headline: Traces of Justice turns decades of forensic work into a crime thriller
content.shortHeadline: Traces of Justice follows a forensic scientist across decades
content.standfirst: Chen Sicheng’s feature draws on the career of real forensic scientist Cui Daozhi, adapting him into a fictional investigator. Its cases chart changing police methods while combining procedural puzzles with a more complicated portrait of law enforcement.

image.caption: A scene from Traces of Justice.

sources.originalTitle: Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller

segments.body: Traces of Justice follows Cui Xun, a fictional investigator based on forensic scientist Cui Daozhi, known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. The film moves through cases from the 1970s to the 1990s, showing how techniques once considered novel become routine as forensic work changes.

segments.title: More than a casebook
segments.body: The review praises the film’s forensic puzzles and set pieces, while noting a tension between its crime-solving story and its portrayal of Chinese law enforcement. Its ending credits also connect Cui’s work to present-day surveillance schemes, leaving the film’s celebration of investigative progress with a sharper edge.

content.headline: Soul Patrol honours an all-Black Vietnam reconnaissance team and its cost
content.shortHeadline: Soul Patrol tells the story of a Black unit in Vietnam
content.standfirst: This documentary follows six young African American soldiers sent behind enemy lines, and the racism they faced at home and in the military. It also meets survivors again decades later, after many had lived with trauma in silence.

image.caption: A still from Soul Patrol.

sources.originalTitle: Soul Patrol review – heartstopping story of the US army’s first Black special ops team at work in Vietnam

segments.body: Soul Patrol tells the story of a six-man all-Black Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol in Vietnam. The young soldiers carried heavy loads behind enemy lines to report on Vietcong movements. The documentary draws on unit member Ed Emanuel’s memoir and includes the men’s later reunion.

segments.title: The danger beyond the mission
segments.body: The film describes how the unit’s skill and bravery coexisted with what some members came to see as racist exploitation, with Black soldiers used as cannon fodder. Some had volunteered partly to escape racism on the home front, only to return carrying anger and post-traumatic stress for decades.

content.headline: Wicker’s bawdy fairy tale makes a provocative joke of perfect devotion
content.shortHeadline: Wicker is a funny, uneasy fairy tale about a made-to-order husband
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a woman who pays for a husband woven from willow. The review delights in the film’s comic excess while questioning the central fantasy of a partner whose life seems entirely organised around pleasing her.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman commissions a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to make her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s wickerwork creation is immediately devoted to her, prompting both comic bedroom scenes and envy among the village’s other women.

segments.title: The joke and its limits
segments.body: The review calls the film funny and knowingly sexist, asking what it means to imagine a partner with little apparent agency of his own. It suggests the fantasy lands partly because the fisherwoman experiences his patience and support as a relief from a world where women are expected to be subordinate.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve recalls the role that changed her plans to leave acting
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the film that changed her career
content.standfirst: Reinsve says she was preparing to give up acting when Joachim Trier offered her the lead in The Worst Person in the World. She reflects on the film’s honesty, its reception and the very different role she plays in Fjord.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': Renate Reinsve on her life-changing role in The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve thought The Worst Person in the World would be her last film before she walked its Cannes red carpet in 2021. Joachim Trier had offered her the lead just after she decided to leave acting; the film’s success and her best-actress prize changed her career.

segments.title: Finding compassion in a new role
segments.body: Reinsve says the film’s playful shoot in Oslo was her favourite, and that Julie’s uncertainties felt familiar. In her latest role, in Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord, she plays Lisbet, a quiet evangelical Christian whose children are removed on suspicion of abuse. Reinsve says she wanted to understand the character without judging her.

content.headline: I Play Rocky retells how Sylvester Stallone fought to play his own creation
content.shortHeadline: I Play Rocky revisits Stallone’s fight to star in Rocky
content.standfirst: A new film recounts how Stallone wrote the story of a boxer who refuses to give up, then resisted studio efforts to cast another actor. The account connects his struggle to Rocky Balboa’s underdog appeal.

sources.originalTitle: 'It was a total miracle': How rejection led Sylvester Stallone to create film's ultimate underdog Rocky

segments.body: I Play Rocky tells the story of Sylvester Stallone’s push to write and star in Rocky. The film portrays an aspiring actor with little money drafting the screenplay in three days, then insisting on playing Balboa even as the studio offered more money for the script if a better-known star took the lead.

segments.title: Why the underdog endured
segments.body: The film’s contributors connect Stallone’s fight for the role to Rocky’s story of persistence. The boxer loses his bout with Apollo Creed, but the review’s interviewees argue that the ending makes the film’s appeal less about winning than about refusing to be counted out.

content.headline: Women accuse David Walliams of grooming and harassment; he denies the claims
content.shortHeadline: Women accuse David Walliams; he denies the allegations
content.standfirst: A Guardian and ITV News investigation reports allegations from women who say Walliams pursued them when they were teenagers or young adults and behaved inappropriately at work. Walliams denies grooming, harassment and wrongdoing.

image.caption: Composite illustration for the investigation into allegations against David Walliams.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It wasn’t long until he asked me if I’d ever had sex before’: David Walliams accused of preying on young women for sex

segments.body: Women interviewed by the Guardian and ITV News allege that David Walliams used his celebrity status to pursue them for sex, including some who say he contacted them when they were teenagers. The investigation also reports claims of inappropriate behaviour towards women at Britain’s Got Talent and his publisher HarperCollins.

segments.title: His response
segments.body: Walliams denies being a sexual predator, grooming women or abusing his power. His lawyers say he understood one woman to be 18 when they resumed contact and dispute her account; he says he regrets behaving thoughtlessly towards people he had casual sexual relationships with. The investigation reports that HarperCollins ended its publishing relationship with him after concerns were raised about his behaviour.

content.headline: Rivals returns with more than 30 romps and plenty of 1980s excess
content.shortHeadline: Rivals’ 10 most outrageous sex scenes, revisited
content.standfirst: As the series returns, this exuberant guide revisits memorable encounters from its first run, from a mid-air tryst to outdoor antics. Its jokes lean into the show’s deliberately over-the-top take on desire and privilege.

image.caption: Alex Hassell as Rupert Campbell-Black and Victoria Smurfit as Maud O’Hara in Rivals.

sources.originalTitle: Shower orgasms, golf carts, spread-eagled on the stairs – it’s the 10 best Rivals sex scenes so far

segments.body: The Guardian’s rundown of Rivals’ sex scenes treats the series as a comic parade of 1980s excess. The selection ranges from Rupert Campbell-Black’s mid-air encounter to a messy outdoor montage, with the article counting 33 sex scenes across the episodes covered.

segments.title: A bonkbuster with a bite
segments.body: The piece acknowledges that Rivals also takes aim at the era’s social and political mores, but argues that its most persistent pleasure is its bawdy spectacle. Its descriptions are deliberately irreverent, reflecting the adaptation’s mix of melodrama and sexual comedy.

content.headline: Mums v Big Pharma follows the campaign that exposed sodium valproate risks
content.shortHeadline: Two mothers’ campaign brought sodium valproate risks to light
content.standfirst: A documentary follows Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, whose efforts to understand their children’s disabilities helped uncover failures to warn about epilepsy drug sodium valproate. The review notes that promised compensation has yet to reach affected families.

image.caption: Emma Murphy and Janet Williams.

sources.originalTitle: Mums v Big Pharma review – the ‘bored, hysterical housewives’ who exposed a horrifying scandal

segments.body: Mums v Big Pharma follows Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, who began investigating after their children were diagnosed with disabilities following exposure to sodium valproate, also known by the brand name Epilim. Their questions led them to other families and to evidence about the drug’s risks.

segments.title: Warnings, and what came next
segments.body: The review recounts research linking sodium valproate exposure to risks of physical malformations and serious neurodevelopmental disorders, and the discovery of an official response that feared warnings would cause women “fruitless anxiety”. It says a promised state compensation scheme has still not paid the estimated 20,000 affected families.

content.headline: Kerr Smith remembers Dawson’s Creek’s first primetime gay kiss
content.shortHeadline: Kerr Smith on Dawson’s Creek and its landmark kiss
content.standfirst: In a new memoir, the actor revisits playing Jack McPhee, the protests around his coming-out story and the first kiss between two men on US primetime network television. He also recounts homophobic harassment he had kept private.

image.caption: Kerr Smith and fellow Dawson’s Creek cast members in 2000.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We did 10 takes of it!’ Kerr Smith on Dawson’s Creek and filming US TV’s first gay kiss

segments.body: Kerr Smith says playing Jack McPhee on Dawson’s Creek remains difficult to match in his career. His new memoir revisits the character’s coming-out storyline and the kiss with Adam Kaufman’s Ethan, which Smith describes as the first between two men on US primetime network television.

segments.title: The response off screen
segments.body: The storyline drew protests outside the show’s Wilmington studio. Smith says he was also the target of homophobic graffiti on his car while filming elsewhere, an incident he had not previously discussed. He says a new generation of viewers still tells him the Jack storyline mattered to them.

content.headline: Rivals, 12 12 12 and more: the shows worth streaming this week
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: Rivals, 12 12 12 and five more picks
content.standfirst: The week’s recommendations span the return of Rivals, a bank-heist thriller and a City of God follow-up. The guide also picks a Lord of the Rings prequel and several true-crime and family-friendly options.

image.caption: Bella Maclean as Taggie O’Hara and Alex Hassell as Rupert Campbell-Black in Rivals.

sources.originalTitle: Rivals to 12 12 12: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Guardian’s weekly guide leads with Rivals, which returns amid bereavement, family tensions and a contest over television rights. It also recommends 12 12 12, a Zurich bank-heist series that unfolds across the year of planning, the hours of the robbery and the days of the police investigation.

segments.title: More to watch
segments.body: Other selections include the second season of City of God, a Lord of the Rings prequel, two true-crime series and a Peanuts holiday animation. The guide notes that City of God has become more episodic in its move to television, while still retaining its force.

content.headline: Tonight’s television: a documentary asks whether penis enhancement is next
content.shortHeadline: Tonight on TV: male insecurity and penis enhancement surgery
content.standfirst: A Storyville documentary follows a businessman seeking to bring penis-enhancement surgery into the mainstream, without judging its participants. The evening’s other picks include a symphony series and a crime investigation in Wales.

image.caption: A still from Storyville: Manhood.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: a documentary about penis enhancement surgery

segments.body: Storyville’s documentary considers whether penis-enhancement surgery is a response to male insecurity or an attempt to profit from it. The guide says the film takes a nonjudgmental approach to Dallas businessman Bill Moore, who is trying to bring the procedures into wider use.

segments.title: Other evening picks
segments.body: The listings also recommend a television series examining five symphonies, beginning with Holst’s The Planets, and a crime documentary relocating to south Wales. Other options include a domestic reality series and a compilation of television mishaps.

content.headline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife, caring for her mother and ageing on screen
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife and caring for her mother
content.standfirst: After 15 years playing Shelagh, Main is taking a break from Call the Midwife and appearing in a play about Elizabeth II. She discusses helping care for her mother and why she wanted her character to age naturally.

image.caption: Laura Main in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Laura Main has not filmed Call the Midwife this year, as the series takes a break before a planned 16th season. She is touring in By Royal Appointment, a play about Elizabeth II, while also helping to care for her 91-year-old mother in Aberdeen.

segments.title: Letting Shelagh grow older
segments.body: Main says she wanted Shelagh to age at the natural rate, even when she herself might have preferred to slow the passage of time. She also describes the support her family has received from Aberdeen council and the difficulty many carers face in balancing work with long-term care.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into The Split’s legal-drama world
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up refreshes the family-law drama in Manchester
content.standfirst: The new spin-off follows a British Asian family at a Manchester divorce-law firm. Its creators and cast discuss representation, the show’s mix of professional cases and family conflict, and the next generation shaping the series.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up moves the family-law drama to Manchester, where Ritu Arya plays barrister Aria Kishan, whose father’s changed succession plans unsettle her future at the family firm. The series follows the cases the lawyers handle as well as the disputes within their own family.

segments.title: Representation and continuity
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to portray a British Asian family in ordinary, contemporary circumstances rather than make them representatives of every aspect of a culture. Original series creator Abi Morgan says the spin-off keeps the franchise’s interest in family and relationship breakdown while making space for a new creative team.

content.headline: Titanium Court turns 8-bit fairies and surprise songs into a singular game
content.shortHeadline: Titanium Court is a strange, delightful game of surprises
content.standfirst: AP Thomson’s game combines a strategy puzzle, a fairy court and optional musical detours, with no guarantee that the next scene will make sense. Its appeal, the writer argues, is the pleasure of not knowing what comes next.

image.caption: A scene from Titanium Court.

sources.originalTitle: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

segments.body: Titanium Court begins as a tile-matching strategy game in a fairy castle, but its 8-bit world soon veers into unexpected territory. In one encounter, a boss fight gives way to an optional song by developer AP Thomson, who says he learned guitar to make music for the game.

segments.title: The pleasure of not knowing
segments.body: Thomson describes fairies as a way to explore strange ideas without conventional rules. The review argues that the game’s shifting logic, theatrical framing and peculiar details make discovery its central pleasure, and says its appeal endured beyond the writer’s hospital stay that first introduced them to it.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a lost future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure means no new Mass Effect from the studio
content.standfirst: The writer reflects on EA’s closure of the studio and cancellation of its forthcoming Mass Effect game, alongside more than 400 job losses. The personal account explains why the original trilogy’s characters and choices still resonate.

image.caption: A scene from Mass Effect 3.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The writer reports that EA has closed BioWare, cancelled its forthcoming Mass Effect game and put more than 400 people out of work. The studio, known for role-playing games including Mass Effect, Dragon Age and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, had a 30-year history.

segments.title: A story shaped by players
segments.body: The writer describes returning repeatedly to the original Mass Effect trilogy, drawn back by its characters and the way choices could carry across games. The loss of the studio, the article argues, means not only the end of a developer but the disappearance of a possible continuation of a world fans had helped shape.

content.headline: A father and son return to the first game they played together
content.shortHeadline: Playing Call of Duty with his son brings one dad to tears
content.standfirst: Replaying Modern Warfare 2’s co-op missions gives a father and his 22-year-old son a chance to revisit an early gaming bond. Their renewed teamwork turns old failures into a source of joy—and a farewell memory before they move apart.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the writer played with his son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: A father and his 22-year-old son return to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together when the son was five. They tackle co-op missions they never completed in childhood, learning to balance the father’s cautious approach with his son’s more impulsive play.

segments.title: A game as shared time
segments.body: The pair eventually beat missions that had defeated them years earlier, and the father reflects on gaming as a rare chance to spend unhurried time together. With the two due to move to different parts of the world, his son tells him he expects to remember these weeks as some of their best times together.

content.headline: CAR-T therapy brings early improvement for some with stiff person syndrome
content.shortHeadline: CAR-T shows early promise for stiff person syndrome
content.standfirst: A small early trial reported major improvements in some people with the rare autoimmune disorder, including a return to work and everyday activities. Researchers say it remains unknown whether the benefits will last.

sources.originalTitle: Medical breakthrough offers hope to people with same stiff person syndrome as Céline Dion

segments.body: Doctors at the Mayo Clinic report that some participants with stiff person syndrome (SPS) improved after CAR-T cell therapy, a treatment already used for some cancers. Patients who had struggled to walk or manage daily tasks were able to resume activities; one returned to work and hobbies.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The treatment uses patients’ T cells, engineered to target disease-causing cells. Neurologist Anastasia Zekeridou called the improvements striking, but said the key question is whether they will be sustained. The report describes early results, not a cure or established treatment for SPS.

content.headline: Weight-loss drug boom could put insulin access at risk, report warns
content.shortHeadline: Weight-loss drug boom raises concerns over insulin access
content.standfirst: A medicines-access group warns that commercial focus on lucrative GLP-1 drugs may draw attention from basic diabetes care. Many people in lower-income countries still struggle to obtain insulin, while new weight-loss medicines remain costly or unavailable.

image.caption: GLP-1 medicines including Mounjaro, Wegovy and Ozempic.

sources.originalTitle: Pharma firms’ focus on weight-loss drugs could put insulin supply at risk, experts warn

segments.body: The Access to Medicine Foundation says the rush into GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic and Mounjaro risks diverting pharmaceutical companies’ attention from treatments including insulin. The group says access to basic insulin remains a serious problem, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

segments.title: Unequal access
segments.body: An estimated 589 million adults worldwide have diabetes, 81% of them in low- and middle-income countries, according to the report. It says GLP-1 medicines are not registered in many poorer countries, and where available their prices can put them beyond reach. The foundation also warns that companies could leave the insulin market, though it presents this as a risk rather than a decision already made.

content.headline: Climate change may alter lightning and the fires it helps ignite
content.shortHeadline: How a warming climate could change lightning and fire
content.standfirst: Lightning is a vital part of Earth’s systems and a major source of wildfire ignition. Research reviewed in this feature suggests it may increase in some regions as the climate warms, but projections vary widely.

sources.originalTitle: Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?

segments.body: Lightning helps drive ecological and atmospheric processes, but it can also ignite fires, including in remote areas that are difficult to reach. The feature describes how intense fires can generate their own lightning-producing storm systems, which may spread fire through new strikes and wind-driven embers.

segments.title: A wide range of projections
segments.body: A review of studies, still under peer review, found estimates ranging from an 11% decrease to a 44% increase in lightning per degree of global warming, with a mean projected increase of 7.5%. Researchers point to significant uncertainty in the models and long-term data; fire risk also depends on conditions such as dryness, wind and heat.

content.headline: Vascular dementia may be under-recognised, and early prevention matters
content.shortHeadline: Vascular dementia may be missed, researchers warn
content.standfirst: Vascular damage can contribute to memory loss alongside Alzheimer’s disease, and may be missed in some diagnoses. Specialists say blood-pressure control and other measures that protect blood vessels could reduce risk.

sources.originalTitle: The little-known blood pressure pill benefits that could be dementia game-changer

segments.body: Vascular dementia is often described as responsible for 20% to 30% of dementia cases, but the i Paper’s report says it may be under-recognised, particularly when it occurs alongside Alzheimer’s. Researchers also describe a possible overlap: impaired blood-vessel function may hinder the removal of waste from the brain, while amyloid can accumulate in vessel walls.

segments.title: Prevention and research
segments.body: Specialists say controlling high blood pressure, avoiding smoking, keeping active and managing cholesterol can help protect blood vessels and may reduce the chance of progressing from mild memory problems to dementia. Two drugs used to widen blood vessels are being tested in UK trials; they are not yet established treatments for vascular dementia.

content.headline: Palantir pressed a UK minister to expand its NHS data reach to GP records
content.shortHeadline: Palantir lobbied to bring GP records into its NHS platform
content.standfirst: Messages obtained under freedom-of-information law show the company urged a former health minister to consider adding GP data to its NHS platform, despite earlier assurances that primary-care records were outside the contract’s scope.

sources.originalTitle: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

segments.body: WhatsApp messages between Palantir’s UK boss and former health minister Zubir Ahmed show the company arguing that linking GP and hospital data could benefit the NHS. The correspondence, obtained by campaign group Foxglove, concerned Foundry, Palantir’s platform under a £330m NHS England contract that had expressly excluded GP data.

segments.title: Trust and scope
segments.body: Doctors and patient groups have opposed adding GP records, citing concerns about trust, transparency and access to sensitive personal information. The British Medical Association warns that identifiable data could undermine the doctor-patient relationship. Palantir says it is for government to decide how its software is used and that NHS organisations retain local control of their data; the Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

content.headline: Fridge hacks expose old cyber flaws as experts debate wider threat
content.shortHeadline: Fridge hacks expose old cyber flaws and uncertain attribution
content.standfirst: Cyberattacks that disrupted commercial refrigerators across Europe exploited weak security, according to reporting on the incidents. France blamed Iran, while other accounts describe uncertainty over whether the attacks were linked and what they signal.

image.caption: Empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Paris after the cyberattack.

sources.originalTitle: The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes
Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?

segments.body: France attributed an attack on supermarket refrigerators to hackers operating under Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The disruption spoiled food and, in some cases, refrigerators became hot enough to catch fire. A cybersecurity expert cited by the Guardian said the hackers used default passwords and that attacks on refrigeration systems elsewhere in Europe were presumed to be linked.

segments.title: Old systems, new concerns
segments.body: The wider reporting describes disagreement over attribution: one expert saw possible Russian traits but said the evidence was not conclusive. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warns AI could help attackers find weaknesses, but officials said AI was not needed to exploit the refrigerator systems’ published default passwords. Some affected equipment was old and no longer receiving security updates.

content.headline: Ukraine seeks more independent access to space as war reaches orbit
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine builds space capability as war reaches orbit
content.standfirst: As satellites underpin communications, drones and battlefield intelligence, Ukraine is trying to reduce reliance on foreign systems and develop its own capabilities. The conflict is also exposing gaps in international rules for space.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war

segments.body: Ukraine’s August strike on a Russian rocket and space centre in Samara highlighted how the war is reaching infrastructure used to support satellite networks. Russia is also rapidly deploying its Rassvet system after being shut out of Starlink, while Ukrainian forces depend heavily on space-based communications and intelligence.

segments.title: Building alternatives
segments.body: Ukraine and Denmark’s GomSpace announced the launch of Obria Nano, a test satellite for a planned independent Ukrainian communications network. Kyiv says it has tested near-space interception systems, but funding and production remain challenges. Experts interviewed by the Guardian say commercial providers and the expansion of military activity are testing outdated, hard-to-enforce space treaties.

content.headline: N-able takes remote-management service offline after zero-day disclosure
content.shortHeadline: N-able takes service offline after zero-day bugs disclosed
content.standfirst: The company has taken its hosted N-Central service offline and urged customers running it themselves to do the same after a researcher published vulnerabilities that could expose credentials and administrator access.

sources.originalTitle: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes dozens of zero-day bugs

segments.body: N-able says it has taken its cloud-hosted N-Central service offline while it works on security fixes. The service lets business customers remotely manage devices and systems on their networks. The company also urged customers with self-hosted deployments to take them down, warning that published exploits could put those networks at risk.

Researcher Ben Bales published the flaws online without giving the company advance notice, according to TechCrunch. He described them as enabling credential theft, new administrator accounts and root access. N-able says it has no evidence that attackers successfully exploited the vulnerabilities, but the outage means customers cannot use the service while remediation is under way.

content.headline: Apple TV adds sign-language interpretation to selected original films
content.shortHeadline: Apple TV adds sign-language interpretation to selected films
content.standfirst: The new feature lets viewers turn on American or British Sign Language interpretation within supported Apple TV titles. Apple says it worked with Deaf-community specialists on the interpretations and is not using AI-generated interpreters.

image.caption: Being Heumann is the first Apple TV original to debut with sign-language interpretation.

sources.originalTitle: Apple TV Adds Sign Language Interpretation, Starting With Original Film ‘Being Heumann’
Apple TV makes sign language interpretation a built-in accessibility feature

segments.body: Apple TV’s sign-language option begins with the film Being Heumann and is set to extend to other titles. Viewers can select an available language in settings, then activate interpretation for supported films from within the player. The interpreter appears on screen alongside the main title rather than in a separate version of the film.

segments.title: Human interpretation
segments.body: Apple says it worked with Directors of Artistic Sign Language to match interpretations to each film’s tone. The company is not using AI-generated interpreters, saying this is not what Deaf audiences have asked for. A CNET report adds that sign languages are still less widely available in entertainment than captions, and that interpretation depends on skilled human professionals.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch reports that Apple chose not to use AI-generated interpreters, citing feedback from the Deaf community, and describes the feature as integrated with the film rather than a separate product.

content.headline: Anthropic targets up to $1.4tn valuation in stock-market listing
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic targets up to $1.4tn valuation in IPO
content.standfirst: The Claude developer’s proposed share price would value it below the $2tn figure previously discussed by backers. Its filing also details a large private share sale and substantial spending commitments as investors weigh the durability of the AI boom.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation
